paragraphs.text: The University of Otago's Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study is one of the most famous studies in the world. Often simply referred to as The Dunedin Study, it has been following the lives of 1,037 people born between April 1, 1972 and March 31, 1973 in Dunedin's Queen Mary Maternity Hospital. At regular intervals, 12 times so far, these study members are brought back to Dunedin, New Zealand, from wherever in the world they live – at the last assessment only a third still lived in the city of Dunedin itself – to participate in a day of interviews, physical tests, computer questionnaires and surveys.

The Dunedin Study was established in order to provide us with answers to questions on subjects as diverse as child health, injury prevention and criminality. It asks whether life's outcomes are the product of nature or nurture. Why, for example, does one person end up heading a successful business while another repeatedly heads to court? The findings of The Dunedin Study are broadly the same as those of research work that began much later in other developed countries, which is why it has long been regarded as one of the very best within the field. So respected is the study, and such is the worldwide interest in its findings, at least from social scientists, that it has had a major impact on global thinking and social policy-making in areas such as healthcare and the justice system.

Professor Terrie Moffitt is now the study's associate director. When she first joined the other study researchers in 1986, she was interested in the statistics on youth crime. Using data obtained from the early days of the study, she found that there was a clear connection between disruptive, bullying behaviour at the age of three and criminal offending in the same study participants in later years. However, she also found that by age 25, the majority of those study members who had occasionally engaged in shoplifting or vandalising property had grown out of this kind of lifestyle. 'They were the ones who were high-spirited, curious and lively, with good family support,' Moffitt says. 'They didn't like their parents telling them what to do, but after they have moved on or finished education, they might get a good job, a nice partner and settle down to become an upstanding member of the community.'

While many research programmes are financed by corporations hoping to eventually profit from a new product or policy, this is not the case with the Dunedin Study. For this reason, its findings are seen as highly reliable. But despite Moffitt and her team's excellent work, few outside the worlds of science or social policy have heard of The Dunedin Study, or understand how it affects us all. Moffitt now hopes to make the research more widely accessible.

Some of the information she hopes to make available may be surprising to the general public. For a start, there is the fact that thumb-sucking in early childhood is a passing phase with no long-lasting psychological significance. And for parents who are worried that their young children might not be clever enough to gain success in adulthood, it is actually the ability to stay in control of your emotions and moods that indicates whether or not this can be achieved. Moffitt is also keen to make known the effects of television: children who sit and watch it for more than two hours a day are more likely to suffer depression as they get older; another reason to limit this passive activity. Another of the study's discoveries is that living around cats or dogs or other domestic creatures may decrease the incidence of asthma, a health issue that is on the rise in many countries.

When they had reached their twenties, study members were asked to bring their partners to an assessment. The results suggested that we choose someone whose personality is much like our own, and this may or may not be an unconscious decision. Researchers also observed how the language the study member and his or her partner used was at a very comparable level of sophistication.

As the study members age, lead researchers focus on learning about new areas. Where once they were experts in early childhood, they later looked at behaviour in social relationships, criminality and parenting practices. Now, with the study members having reached middle age, the researchers are looking at new areas again. The aim of one extensive questionnaire is to find out how stressed study participants are, and to see how work has contributed to this kind of anxiety. Another survey has been designed to see how people feel about their retirement, and to discover if and how they are preparing financially for this event.

Soon, study participants will return for the next round of testing. Members will undergo an eight-hour day of testing, including dental examinations and tests to see what allergies may have developed since their last visit. Researchers can see about four people a day, so processing all participants will take 18 months to two years. No doubt the results will be fascinating.
